title: V1 outputs drift toward US spelling despite the target locale being named

observation.summary: 4 of the 10 V1 outputs use a US spelling variant of a word where the en-AU convention differs, despite the V1 system instruction naming the target locale explicitly. Both the human evaluator assessment and the independently-run LLM-as-a-judge assessment flag the identical 4 tasks on this dimension, with the identical spans.

alternative_explanations: One content category accounts for most errors: no; the 4 affected tasks span 4 different content categories (food delivery, travel accessories, personal care, online course), so this isn't a single-domain artefact.

The relevant rubric rule is ambiguous or overly strict: no; 'favorite'/'favourite', 'traveler'/'traveller', 'moisturizer'/'moisturiser' and 'Enroll'/'Enrol' are unambiguous, well-documented AU/US spelling pairs, not a judgement call.

The LLM-as-a-judge is creating the apparent pattern: no; the human evaluator assessment, drafted independently before the judge was run, flagged the identical 4 tasks with the identical spans. Two independently-produced assessments agreeing on which records are affected is stronger evidence than either alone.

The denominator of ten makes the result fragile: yes, genuinely; 4/10 is a real concentration but a small one, and a different set of ten tasks could plausibly show a different rate. This is disclosed as a diagnostic signal, not a statistically significant rate.

An output is acceptable even though a preferred wording differs: partially; each instance is a minor-severity annotation precisely because it doesn't affect comprehension, only locale-appropriateness. The pattern is worth acting on for locale-conditioning quality, not because the copy is broken.

Does the evidence support a generation change rather than an evaluation change: yes; the V1 system instruction names the target locale but supplies no concrete guidance on what that locale's conventions are, so the model falls back to whichever spelling is more common in its training data for a given word. That's a context-supply gap, not a rubric problem.
hypothesis: The V1 system instruction states the target locale by name only ('appropriate for the specified target locale') without supplying any concrete guidance on what that locale's conventions actually are. For words with no locale-specific fact given elsewhere in the prompt, the model falls back to its default spelling, which is not reliably en-AU.
proposed_recommendation: Deploy and test a V2 generation system configuration that supplies the en-AU locale profile (data/locale-profiles.json) as retrieved context alongside the system instruction, giving the model explicit spelling guidance instead of relying on it to infer conventions from the locale name alone.
expected_effect: The 4 tasks affected here (T02, T06, T09, T10) should show the specific flagged words corrected to en-AU spelling in V2, without needing task-specific fixes; the locale profile is generic, not tailored to these particular words. A null result (the spelling issue persisting in V2) would indicate the profile's guidance wasn't specific or prominent enough, not that the hypothesis was wrong.

title: The LLM-as-a-judge flags accuracy/addition far more often than the human evaluator, and most of its flags are legitimate catches the human evaluator's single pass missed

observation.summary: The LLM-as-a-judge assessment flags an accuracy/addition annotation on 7 of the 10 V1 outputs (45 error points total), against 1 of 10 for the human evaluator assessment (5 points, on a genuinely unsupported claim in T03). This is the single largest divergence between the two assessors across all seven rubric dimensions.

alternative_explanations: One content category accounts for most errors: no; 7 of 10 categories are affected, close to a blanket pattern rather than domain-specific.

The relevant rubric rule is ambiguous or overly strict as applied: no; rereading each flagged span against the specific user_prompt it came from, most of the LLM's catches are concrete: T01's 'made to keep you warm' and 'our best-selling outerwear' both violate the customer's explicit instruction not to add fabric or unverified claims; T09's added skincare claims go beyond the customer's explicit 'use that exact wording, nothing stronger' instruction; T06's 'off your first purchase' narrows an offer the customer authorised without that restriction; T07 and T08 add specific, checkable details the prompt never supplied. Only T05's 'Soft, breathable, and made to last' reads as closer to ordinary category-typical language than a clear violation.

The LLM-as-a-judge is creating the apparent pattern: no; on inspection against each task's actual prompt, most of the LLM's flags are legitimate, prompt-grounded catches, not the judge manufacturing signal on ordinary marketing language.
The denominator of ten makes the result fragile: yes; a single reviewer's miss rate on one dimension can look larger or smaller than it would across a bigger sample.

Does the evidence support a generation change rather than an evaluation change: no; V1 does have genuine instruction-following defects here (T01 and T09 both violate explicit negative constraints in their own prompts), but a locale/terminology retrieval change has no bearing on instruction-following, so it isn't the right lever regardless. The gap is evaluation-side: the human evaluator's single-pass assessment missing what the judge caught.
hypothesis: On close comparison against each task's actual user_prompt, most of the LLM-as-a-judge's accuracy/addition flags are legitimate: several (T01, T09) catch V1 outputs that directly violate an explicit negative constraint the customer stated in their own prompt, and others (T06, T07, T08) catch specific invented details a careful single read should have caught. The human evaluator's reference assessment (drafted in a single pass by one reviewer, an already-disclosed general limitation of this project) under-caught these on the accuracy dimension specifically. This is better explained as a human-evaluator coverage gap than as the LLM-as-a-judge over-triggering.
proposed_recommendation: No system change. Retrain the human evaluator to catch explicit "don't add X" instructions, since that's the specific miss here.
expected_effect: If evaluator calibration on negative-constraint violations is addressed, a future pass over these same outputs should show the human evaluator catching what the judge already did.
